---
title: "Exercise · Introduction"
---

A short, guided task. Complete it before moving on to the lab.

## Task

Write a one-sentence description of a Pico **in your own words**, and list
three examples of things in your day-to-day work that could plausibly be
modeled as Picos.

::: {.callout-note}
There is no single correct answer. The goal is to internalize the
"Rules → Parser → Composer → Pico" mental model from the
[lesson](index.qmd).
:::

## Success criteria

- [ ] Your description mentions that a Pico is **declarative** and
      **composable**.
- [ ] You can name at least **three** candidate Picos.
- [ ] For at least one candidate, you can sketch what the Rules might look
      like in YAML.

## Automatable check

If you sketched at least one Rule in YAML, save it as
`rules/<your-slug>.yaml` under a scratch working directory and confirm
it matches the reference Parser's flat `id` / `kind` / `value` shape
using the `pico` CLI shipped in this repository (see the
[Hello Pico one-time setup](../../../../labs/hello-pico/objectives.html#one-time-setup)
for the `PATH` export):

```bash
pico parse rules/<your-slug>.yaml --out /tmp/parsed.json \
  && echo "OK: parsed rules/<your-slug>.yaml"
```

The command exits with status `0` and prints an `OK:` line when the
sketch is well-formed. This is an optional accompaniment to the
reflection questions — the exercise's primary goal remains
internalizing the mental model, but any YAML you draft can now be
mechanically validated.

## Reflect

- Which of your three examples is the simplest to model?
- Which one would be the hardest, and why?
